messages.subject: jittermap genetic map vs cross object
messages.subject_clean: jittermap genetic map vs cross object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Browman,

For some phenotypes, but not others, I get an error when running refineqtl and stepwiseqtl.

refineqtl error: In scanqtl(cross = cross, pheno.col = pheno.col, chr = chrnam,  ... :
  Confused about QTL positions.  You should probably run jittermap to ensure that no two markers conincide.

stepwiseqtl error: makeqtl(cross, chr, pos.tmp, what = "prob") :
  Multiple markers at the same position; run jittermap

When I ran summary.scanone on the scanone output, I noticed that the marker positions were rounded. I changed the digits used in the summary so that all the decimal places are included for each position, but this didn't fix the error. It was surprising though that the positions were rounded.

I then ran summary.cross and got an this error.
  In summary.cross(cross.obj) :
    Some markers at the same position on chr 2,3,5,7,9; use jittermap().

When I ran jittermap on the cross object right before running refineqtl/stepwiseqtl, they ran fine and I didn't get the error message.

What is bothering me the most about this is that I ran jittermap on the genetic map and removed duplicate markers before I made the cross object, so I know that there aren't duplicate markers in the map.

Should I only run jittermap once the cross object is made? Adding phenotypic data shouldn't change the marker positions, should it?

Any help you can provide would be greatly appreciated.

Rachel

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] jittermap genetic map vs cross object
messages.body_plain:
You should just need to run jittermap once, at the very beginning.
Be sure to assign it back to the object, so that you're working with
the version where markers are moved slightly so as to not be exactly
overlapping.

  mycross <- jittermap(mycross)

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] singular matricex using cim()
messages.body_plain:
Hello Dr. Broman,

I am having a similar issue when I run the cim() function using the "ehk" method. The code is given below:

#### loading the data and calculating genoprob. I am running the analysis on a RIL population by selfing.

Rqtl.data = read.cross("csv", "F:/LAB_WORK/WUENUE/GRxI_QTL_R/", "my_pheno_geno_data.csv", alleles = c("A", "B"), genotypes = c("AA", "BB"))

Rqtl.data <- convert2riself(Rqtl.data)

grxi.genoprob = calc.genoprob(Rqtl.data, step = 1, error.prob = 0.001)

#### running cim() on all my traits

phen.col = 2:35

n.phe = length(phen.col)

 ehk.cim <- ehk.cim.p1000 <- vector("list", n.phe)

 thr.ehk <- rep(NA, n.phe)

for(i in seq(1, length(phen.col), 1)) {

    ehk.cim.p1000[[i]] <- cim(grxi.genoprob, pheno.col = phen.col[i], n.marcovar = 10, window = 15, method = "ehk", n.perm = 20)

  thr.ehk[i] <- summary(ehk.cim.p1000[[i]], alpha = 0.05)

  ehk.cim[[i]] <- cim(grxi.genoprob, pheno.col = phen.col[i], n.marcovar = 10, window = 15, method = "ehk")

}

I get 50 warnings that read:

X'X matrix is singular

And in some warning messages I can get:

Didn't converge at position 141

The position that didn't converge changes each time I run the cim() function

I also tried running calc.genoprob with error.prob = 0.01 but I still get the same warning messages.

Here are some diagnostics I have done:

1)     I do not have any markers with the same allele for all individuals (total 89 individuals)

2)     I do not have any markers in the same genetic position

3)     I do not have markers that are linked in different chromosomes

4)     I do have a pair of individuals that are 90% similar and another pair that are 80% similar genotypically

5)     I have 8 RILs that have between 30 and 40 crossovers

Can you please provide further advice on how to troubleshoot this problem?

Thank you,

Miguel Macias Gonzalez

messages.subject: Permutation strata strategies
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

For QTL analyses, I need to set permutations for S. cerevisiae cross data of two general kinds:

1) tetrads with replicate samples: each replicate has the same genotype as all replicates for that sample, and the tetrad genotypes at most markers are segregated 2:2. Replicates of each sample are in consecutive rows, and each tetrad is defined by a set of 4 consecutive samples. Permutation strata are within tetrads, so that any individual sample may be swapped with any other sample in the given tetrad, even if the two samples are replicates.

2) non-tetradic yeast segregants with replicates: samples are not tetrads, but as before, each replicate has the same genotype as the other replicates of that sample. Each sample is set as a permutation stratum, and its replicates permuted.

Are these the most appropriate way to permute these data? Is there a better approach to stratifying these permutations?

Thanks for your help.

Regards,

Thomas Walsh.

messages.subject: extreme lod scores during ehk regression
messages.subject_clean: extreme lod scores during ehk regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl Broman and group members,

I'm working on an F2 mapping population with selective genotyping (~500 phenotypes with ~50 genotypes from the extremes) and outbred grandparents. I am using the 4way cross genotype notation, including individuals without genoytpes in the analysis, and using a covariate (cytoplasm type) which is well balanced among the extreme phenotypes.

For the most part, the data are behaving relatively well during single QTL analysis. Most of the mapping approaches I have tried (marker regression, standard interval mapping, Haley-Knott regression, multiple imputation) give reasonable and roughly similar patterns of lod scores across the chromosomes. However, when I use extended Haley-Knott regression, I get very strange output in which most markers have a lod score of 400 and some have very small lod scores (400 looks a ceiling). Note that I also get the warning "X'X matrix is singular" during this analysis but not the others (I checked for monomorphic markers but that doesn't appear to be the problem).

Is it possible that the ehk regression is incompatible with the 4way cross notation?

Any insight would be greatly appreciated!
Thanks,
Kate

Best regards,
Eva

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Cross object with map information only?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Cross object with map information only?
messages.body_plain:
There is a "map" object, which is a list, with each component being a vector of marker positions for a given chromosome.

Take a look at the map10 data included with R/qtl:

  library(qtl)
  data(map10)

If you read in your map as a table with chromosome and position (and with marker names as row names),  you'd want to do the reverse of the function map2table().

  maptab <- map2table(map10)

I'd do:

  map <- split(maptab$pos, maptab$chr)
  mar <- split(rownames(maptab), maptab$chr)
  for(i in seq(along=map))
    names(map[[i]]) <- mar[[i]]

You might want to add "map" class; some functions are insistent on that.

  class(map) <- "map"

karl

I have in mind a picture like this "http://www.rqtl.org/graphs/plot.scantwo.html", but even when it has a tutorial, I'm unable to produce my own picture. If you could guide me I will be thankful

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] eQTLs
messages.body_plain:
What I've typically done is take the single largest LOD score on each chromosome for each trait, for those peaks with LOD > some threshold. I'd then do a scatterplot of the genomic position of the transcript vs the QTL position.

You might take a look at the neqtl package, which includes these sorts of plots.
Install it as follows:

  install.packages(devtools)
  library(devtools)
  install_github("atbroman/neqtl")

It includes a vignette, which you may view by typing:

  vignette("neqtl_intro")

regards,
karl

> > I'm working on an F2 mapping population with selective genotyping (~500 phenotypes with ~50 genotypes from the extremes) and outbred grandparents. I am using the 4way cross genotype notation, including individuals without genoytpes in the analysis, and using a covariate (cytoplasm type) which is well balanced among the extreme phenotypes.
> >
> > For the most part, the data are behaving relatively well during single QTL analysis. Most of the mapping approaches I have tried (marker regression, standard interval mapping, Haley-Knott regression, multiple imputation) give reasonable and roughly similar patterns of lod scores across the chromosomes. However, when I use extended Haley-Knott regression, I get very strange output in which most markers have a lod score of 400 and some have very small lod scores (400 looks a ceiling). Note that I also get the warning "X'X matrix is singular" during this analysis but not the others (I checked for monomorphic markers but that doesn't appear to be the problem).

messages.subject: X chromosome LOD threshold=0
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Broman

I contacted you before with some questions about the use of sex as covariate and the definition of a sex linkage group (post: Q re covariates and sex chromosome). Although I'm not defining a sex linkage group anymore, because it still recombine quite a lot, I still have some questions concerning my previous attempts.

My study systems consist on a CP cross, with the presence of sex chromosomes and sexual dimorphism. I have 314 individuals and 655 SNP markers distributed in 12 linkage groups.
Because I have sexual dimorphism in many of the traits I include sex as a covariate.
When I define the X chromosome and run the permutation test with method "em",  perm.Xsp=TRUE and addcovar=sex, for many of the traits the X LOD threshold drops to 0.

I'm not really sure why this happens and what should be done with this result. Could you give some explanation?
I understand that defining the X chromosome include sex as an internal covariate, but I think one can still allowed for phenotypic differences between sexes by adding sex as covariate.

Thanks a lot!

Fernanda
